learn.hook: Why does a rainbow appear after rain? Why does a ball always come back down? Asking 'why?' is where science begins!
points: Science is a way of finding out how the world around us works.
It begins with curiosity: noticing things and wondering about them.
Science is not just a school subject or a list of facts; it is a way of thinking and checking ideas.
Scientists test their ideas and change them when new evidence shows they were wrong.
Anyone can think like a scientist: a farmer, a cook, a doctor or you!

example.q: Meera says, 'Science is only about lab coats and test tubes.' Is she right?
steps: Think of where people use scientific thinking: farmers checking soil, cooks testing recipes, doctors finding the cause of an illness.
Science is a way of observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
This can happen in a kitchen, a garden or a playground, not only in a lab.
example.answer: No. Science is a way of thinking and finding out that we can use anywhere.

learn.reallife: When you wonder why milk boils over, why curd sets faster in summer, or why your shadow is long in the evening, you are thinking like a scientist.

games.title: Science: true or false?
items: Science is a way of finding out how the world works.
Science helps us understand nature by observing and testing.
Only people working in big laboratories can do science.
Anyone who observes carefully, asks questions and tests ideas is doing science.
Being curious and asking questions is an important part of science.
Questions lead us to explore and find answers.
A scientific idea can change when new evidence is found.
Scientists update their ideas when careful tests show something new.
In science, we accept an idea without checking it.
Science tests ideas with observations and experiments before accepting them.

games.title: Who uses science?
pairs: checks which seeds grow best in the soil
tries recipes to see what tastes best
finds out the cause of an illness
studies clouds and wind to forecast rain

quiz.q: Which of these best describes science?
options: A list of facts to memorise
A way of finding out how the world works
quiz.explain: Science is a method of exploring: observing, asking questions and testing ideas to understand the world.
quiz.mistake: Thinks science is only about remembering facts

quiz.q: Tara wonders why ants walk in a line. What is she showing?
quiz.explain: Wondering 'why' about something you notice is curiosity, the starting point of science.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect wondering with the start of science

quiz.q: What should a scientist do if a careful test shows their idea is wrong?
quiz.explain: Science grows by changing ideas when evidence shows they do not fit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks scientists never change their minds

quiz.q: Which of these is a question science can test?
options: Which colour is the most beautiful?
Do bean seeds sprout faster in warm water or cold water?
quiz.explain: We can test sprouting by setting up seeds and observing. The others depend on personal taste.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up personal opinions with questions that can be tested

quiz.q: Where can science be used?
options: In the kitchen, the farm, the hospital and the playground
quiz.explain: Science is everywhere: in cooking, farming, medicine and even sports.
quiz.mistake: Thinks science happens only in special places

quiz.q: Arjun says, 'Science is finished; everything is already known.' What is wrong with this?
options: There are still many questions nobody has answered
Science is only about the past
quiz.explain: Scientists keep discovering new things every year. There is always more to find out.
quiz.mistake: Believes science has already answered everything

quiz.q: Which habit helps you most in science?
quiz.explain: Careful observation and questioning are the heart of scientific thinking.
quiz.mistake: Thinks guessing without checking is enough

quiz.q: A farmer notices that plants near a tree grow less. She tries planting some in sunny spots to compare. What is she doing?
options: Testing her idea, like a scientist
quiz.explain: She noticed something, made a guess (less sunlight) and set up a comparison to check it. That is scientific thinking.
quiz.mistake: Does not realise everyday people use scientific methods

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: 'Someone told me science is just a big book of facts. Is that true? What is science really?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! So science is a way of being curious, asking questions and testing ideas. I can be a scientist too!
teach.nudge: But how do scientists know if an idea is right? What do they do with it?

learn.hook: A good scientist is like a detective: they notice tiny clues that others miss!
points: Observing means using our senses (seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, tasting) carefully to notice things.
Never taste or smell unknown things to observe them; safety comes first.
Instruments like a magnifying glass, a ruler or a thermometer help us observe more exactly.
Good observations are recorded in a notebook with dates, drawings and numbers.
Good questions come from observations, for example: 'Why are the leaves of this plant drooping?'

example.q: Riya sees that the curd at her nani's house in Jaipur sets faster in May than in January. What question could she ask?
steps: Write down the observation: curd sets faster in May.
Think about what is different in May: it is much warmer.
Turn it into a question that can be tested.
example.answer: Does warmth make curd set faster?

learn.reallife: Birdwatchers in India note the birds they see, like the kingfisher or the peacock, with the date and place. Their careful records help scientists know where birds live and travel.

games.title: Observation or opinion?
items: The water in the glass is 200 mL
The ant is carrying a grain of rice
Blue is a nicer colour than red

items.text: We use our ___ to observe things around us.
A ___ glass makes tiny things look bigger.
We write our observations in a ___ so we don't forget them.
We should never ___ an unknown substance to find out what it is.

quiz.q: Which of these is an observation, not an opinion?
options: Neem trees are the prettiest trees
The neem tree in our school is taller than the school wall
quiz.explain: An observation is something we can see or measure. Pretty, boring and love are personal feelings.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up personal feelings with things that can be seen or measured

quiz.q: Which tool helps you observe the tiny parts of a flower?
quiz.explain: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger so we can see details.
quiz.mistake: Picks a measuring tool that measures something else

quiz.q: Why should a scientist record observations in a notebook?
options: So the details are not forgotten and can be compared later
To copy them from a friend
quiz.explain: Writing things down keeps the details safe so they can be checked and compared.
quiz.mistake: Thinks recording is just for neatness

quiz.q: Kabir finds an unknown white powder in the kitchen. What is the SAFE way to observe it?
options: Look at it and ask an adult what it is
quiz.explain: Unknown substances can be harmful. Looking and asking an adult is safe; tasting or sniffing is not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tasting or smelling unknown things is a safe way to observe

quiz.q: Ananya notices that her tomato plant on the windowsill bends towards the window. Which is a good question to ask?
options: Does the plant like my song?
Does the plant bend towards light?
quiz.explain: A good scientific question comes from the observation and can be tested, like placing the plant in different light.
quiz.mistake: Asks a question that cannot be tested

quiz.q: Which sense do you mainly use to observe that a koel is singing?
quiz.explain: A koel's song is a sound, so we observe it by hearing.
quiz.mistake: Matches the wrong sense to a sound

quiz.q: Which is a more exact observation?
quiz.explain: Using a measurement with a unit gives an exact observation that others can check.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a rough description is as exact as a measurement

quiz.q: Why do scientists ask questions after observing?
options: Questions guide what to explore and test next
Questions are not needed in science
quiz.explain: A question gives a clear goal: what do we want to find out?
quiz.mistake: Thinks observation alone is enough without questioning

teach.ask: Gappu peers through a leaf: 'My teacher said scientists observe. What does it mean to observe, and what comes after that?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Notice carefully with my senses, write it down, then ask a good question. I'm a bird detective now!
teach.nudge: And after I notice something, what should I do with it? Just forget it?

learn.hook: Is your guess right or wrong? There is only one way to find out: test it!
points: The scientific method is a step-by-step way of finding answers.
Steps: observe → ask a question → make a guess (hypothesis) → test it with an experiment → look at the results → draw a conclusion.
A hypothesis is a smart guess that can be tested.
In a fair test, we change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
If the results do not support the guess, we make a new guess and test again. That is not failure; it is learning!

example.q: Dev thinks sugar dissolves faster in warm water than in cold water. How can he test it fairly? (Use warm tap water only, with an adult nearby.)
steps: Take two same-sized glasses with the same amount of water: one warm, one cold.
Add one spoon of sugar to each at the same time and stir both the same way.
Change only the temperature of the water; keep everything else the same.
Observe which glass becomes clear first and write down the result.
example.answer: If the sugar disappears first in the warm water, his guess is supported: warm water dissolves sugar faster.

learn.reallife: Doctors testing a new medicine, and farmers trying a new way of watering, use these same steps: guess, test fairly, and check the results.

games.title: Steps of the scientific method
games.prompt: Put the steps in the right order

games.title: Match the step to the example
pairs: Clothes on the line dried quickly on a sunny day
Does sunlight make clothes dry faster?
A wet cloth in the sun will dry before one in the shade
Hang one wet cloth in the sun and one in the shade
The cloth in the sun dried first, so sunlight speeds up drying

quiz.q: What is a hypothesis?
options: A smart guess that can be tested
quiz.explain: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question, which we then test.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a hypothesis is the final proven answer

quiz.q: Which step comes right after asking a question?
quiz.explain: After the question, we suggest a possible answer (hypothesis), then test it.
quiz.mistake: Jumps straight to testing or concluding

quiz.q: Sana wants to test if sunlight helps methi seeds grow. What must she keep the same in both pots?
options: Soil, water and type of seed
quiz.explain: In a fair test, only the thing being tested (sunlight) changes. Soil, water and seed must be the same.
quiz.mistake: Changes more than one thing, so the test is not fair

quiz.q: An experiment shows that a hypothesis was wrong. What should happen next?
options: Make a new hypothesis and test again
quiz.explain: A wrong guess teaches us something. Scientists make a better guess and test again.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a wrong hypothesis means the experiment failed

quiz.q: Which is the LAST step of the scientific method?
quiz.explain: We draw a conclusion after studying the results of the experiment.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the steps

quiz.q: Rohan tests whether salt or sugar dissolves faster. He uses hot water for salt and cold water for sugar. What is wrong?
options: He changed two things, so the test is not fair
quiz.explain: He changed both the substance and the water temperature, so he cannot tell which one caused the difference.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that only one thing should change in a fair test

quiz.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment?
options: Because the first result is always wrong
To check that the result is reliable
quiz.explain: Getting the same result again and again shows the result can be trusted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks repeating means the first try was a mistake

quiz.q: Which hypothesis can be tested?
options: Ice is happy in the freezer
Ice is the most interesting thing
Ice feels sad when it melts
Ice melts faster in a sunny spot than in a shady spot
quiz.explain: We can time ice melting in sun and shade. Feelings like happy or sad cannot be measured.
quiz.mistake: Picks a statement about feelings that cannot be tested

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'I think my feathers dry faster in the sun. How would a scientist check if I'm right?'
teach.praise: Wow! Guess, test fairly by changing only one thing, then look at the results. Science is my new superpower!
teach.nudge: But if I test in sun and shade, should everything else be the same? And how do I decide at the end?

learn.hook: From tiny ants to huge elephants, from soft grass to giant banyan trees: India is bursting with living things!
points: Biodiversity means the huge variety of living things in a place.
India is one of the world's richest countries in plant and animal variety; the Western Ghats and the Himalayas are full of life.

Plants can be grouped by height and stem: herbs (short, soft green stem, like wheat and mint), shrubs (woody stem with branches near the ground, like rose and hibiscus) and trees (tall, with a thick woody trunk, like neem and mango).
Climbers (like money plant and grapevine) climb up with support; creepers (like watermelon and pumpkin) spread along the ground.
Animals also vary: they live in different places, move in different ways and eat different foods.

example.q: A plant in Meena's garden is about her height. It has a hard, woody stem and many branches starting just above the soil. What kind of plant is it?
steps: Herbs are short with soft, green stems; this stem is woody, so it is not a herb.
Trees have one thick trunk with branches high above the ground; this plant branches near the soil.
Medium height, woody stem, branches near the base: that matches a shrub.
example.answer: It is a shrub, like a rose or hibiscus bush.

learn.reallife: On a walk in a park you may spot a peepal tree, a hibiscus shrub, grass, a money plant climbing a wall, squirrels, mynas and butterflies, all in one place. That is biodiversity!

games.title: Match the plant type to its feature
pairs: short with a soft green stem
woody stem, branches near the ground
tall with a thick woody trunk

quiz.q: What does biodiversity mean?
options: The variety of living things in a place
The number of buildings in a city
Only the animals in a zoo
quiz.explain: 'Bio' means life. Biodiversity is the variety of all plants, animals and other living things.
quiz.mistake: Thinks biodiversity means only animals or non-living things

quiz.q: Which plant is a herb?
quiz.explain: Coriander is short with a soft green stem. Mango, peepal and banyan are tall trees.
quiz.mistake: Does not use stem type and height to classify

quiz.q: Which plant is a shrub?
quiz.explain: A rose bush has a woody stem with branches near the ground, so it is a shrub.
quiz.mistake: Confuses shrubs with herbs or trees

quiz.q: A money plant growing up a wall with support is a:
quiz.explain: Plants that need support to climb upward are climbers.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up climbers (go up) and creepers (spread on the ground)

quiz.q: A watermelon plant spreads along the ground. It is a:
quiz.explain: Plants with weak stems that spread along the ground are creepers.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up creepers and climbers

quiz.q: What is special about a tree's stem?
options: It is a thick, hard, woody trunk
quiz.explain: Trees have a strong woody trunk that holds them up tall, with branches higher up.
quiz.mistake: Confuses trees with herbs or creepers

quiz.q: Which of these regions in India is famous for its rich variety of plants and animals?
quiz.explain: The Western Ghats have forests full of many kinds of plants, frogs, birds and other animals.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that forests and mountains hold high biodiversity

quiz.q: Why do we find different animals in different places?
options: Each kind of animal is suited to where it lives
quiz.explain: Animals are suited to their surroundings: fish to water, camels to deserts, yaks to cold mountains.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every animal can live anywhere

teach.ask: Gappu looks around a garden: 'So many plants! Some are tiny, some are huge. How can I tell a herb, a shrub and a tree apart?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Herbs are short and soft, shrubs are bushy and woody, trees are tall with thick trunks. Now I can name my perches!
teach.nudge: What about the stem? How is a tree's stem different from a herb's stem?

learn.hook: Imagine a library with all books thrown in one heap. Grouping living things is like arranging that library!
points: We group living things by features they share, which makes them easier to study.
Leaves can have net-like veins (reticulate venation, like mango and hibiscus) or parallel veins (parallel venation, like grass, banana and wheat).
Roots can be a taproot (one main root with side roots, like mustard and mango) or fibrous roots (many thin roots of similar size, like wheat, maize and grass).
Plants with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots; plants with net-like venation usually have a taproot.
Seeds of gram and rajma split into two parts (dicots); seeds of maize and wheat have one part (monocots). Animals can be grouped by where they live, how they move or whether they have a backbone.

example.q: Neha finds a plant whose leaves have parallel veins. What kind of roots does it most likely have?
steps: Parallel venation is found in plants like grass, wheat and maize.
These plants have many thin roots coming out from the base of the stem.
So parallel venation usually goes with fibrous roots.
example.answer: Fibrous roots

learn.reallife: Gardeners and farmers group plants to decide how to grow them. Doctors and zoo keepers group animals to understand how to care for them.

games.title: Grouping facts
items: A banana leaf has parallel veins.
Banana leaves have veins running side by side.
A mango leaf has net-like veins.
Wheat has fibrous roots: many thin roots of similar size.
A gram seed can be split into two equal parts.
Gram is a dicot; its seed has two parts.
A maize grain splits into two equal halves.
Maize is a monocot; its seed does not split into two halves.

quiz.q: What kind of venation does a grass leaf have?
quiz.explain: In grass, the veins run side by side along the leaf. This is parallel venation.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up parallel and net-like (reticulate) venation

quiz.q: Which leaf has reticulate (net-like) venation?
quiz.explain: A hibiscus leaf has veins that branch out like a net.
quiz.mistake: Picks a leaf with parallel veins

quiz.q: A taproot is:
options: Many thin roots of the same size
One main root with smaller side roots
A root growing in the air
A root without any branches at all
quiz.explain: A taproot has a thick main root going down, with thin side roots.
quiz.mistake: Confuses taproot with fibrous roots

quiz.q: Which plant has fibrous roots?
quiz.explain: Maize has many thin roots of similar size from the base of the stem.
quiz.mistake: Picks a plant with a taproot

quiz.q: Leaves with net-like veins usually go with which roots?
quiz.explain: Most plants with reticulate venation, like mango and mustard, have a taproot.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the link between venation and roots

quiz.q: Which seed splits into two parts when soaked?
quiz.explain: Soaked gram splits into two parts called cotyledons, so it is a dicot.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cereal grains like wheat and maize are dicots

quiz.q: Which animal has a backbone?
quiz.explain: A frog has a backbone. Earthworms, snails and butterflies do not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks small soft animals have backbones

quiz.q: Why do scientists group living things?
options: To make them easier to study and understand
Because all living things are the same
quiz.explain: Grouping by shared features helps us learn about many living things quickly.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the purpose of classification

teach.ask: Gappu holds two leaves: 'One has lines going side by side, the other looks like a net. What's the difference, and does it tell me anything about roots?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Parallel veins usually mean fibrous roots, and net-like veins usually mean a taproot. I can guess the roots from the leaves!
teach.nudge: Which roots go with which kind of veins? Tell me about taproots and fibrous roots too.

learn.hook: Why does a camel not mind the hot sand, and a fish not drown in water? Nature has given each one special tools!
points: An adaptation is a special feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat (home).
Camel (Thar desert): long legs keep its body away from hot sand, wide padded feet do not sink in sand, and its hump stores fat. It can go many days without drinking water.
Cactus: leaves are turned into spines that reduce water loss; the thick green stem stores water and makes food.
Fish: a streamlined body and fins for swimming, and gills to take in oxygen dissolved in water.
Mountains: deodar and pine trees are cone-shaped with sloping branches so snow slides off; yaks and snow leopards have thick fur to keep warm. Lotus leaves float on water.

example.q: A camel's hump is often said to be a water tank. Is that correct?
steps: Think about what a hump is made of: it is a store of fat.
When food is scarce, the camel's body uses this fat for energy.
Camels can go many days without water for other reasons, such as losing very little water from their bodies.
example.answer: No. The hump stores fat, not water.

learn.reallife: When you visit Ladakh you may see yaks with shaggy coats, and in Rajasthan, camels carrying people across sand dunes. Each animal is built for its home.

games.title: Match the living thing to its adaptation
pairs: long legs and padded feet for hot sand
gills to breathe oxygen dissolved in water
cone shape so snow slides off
long thick hair to keep warm

items.text: A camel's hump stores ___.
Fish breathe using ___.
In a cactus, the leaves are changed into ___.
The surroundings where a living thing lives are its ___.

quiz.q: What is an adaptation?
options: A change of house by an animal
A feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat
quiz.explain: Adaptations, like a fish's gills or a camel's long legs, help living things survive where they live.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adaptation means moving to a new place

quiz.q: What does a camel's hump store?
quiz.explain: The hump stores fat, which the camel's body can use for energy when food is scarce.
quiz.mistake: Believes the common myth that the hump stores water

quiz.q: Why do cacti have spines instead of broad leaves?
options: To soak up rain through the spines
quiz.explain: Broad leaves lose a lot of water. Spines lose very little, which helps in a dry desert.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect spines with saving water

quiz.q: Which part helps a fish breathe in water?
quiz.explain: Gills take in oxygen that is dissolved in water.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up gills with fins, which help in swimming

quiz.q: Why are deodar and pine trees cone-shaped with sloping branches?
options: So that birds cannot sit on them
So that snow slides off easily
quiz.explain: Snow slides off the sloping branches instead of piling up and breaking them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the shape is meant to collect snow

quiz.q: Which animal is best suited to the cold mountains of Ladakh?
quiz.explain: A yak's long, thick hair keeps it warm in the cold mountains.
quiz.mistake: Picks an animal adapted to a different habitat

quiz.q: How does the streamlined shape of a fish help it?
options: It helps the fish climb trees
It helps the fish move easily through water
It helps the fish breathe air
It keeps the fish warm in snow
quiz.explain: A streamlined body is smooth and pointed at the ends, so water flows past it easily.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the purpose of body shape with breathing

quiz.q: Which habitat is a lotus plant adapted to?
quiz.explain: Lotus leaves float on water, and the plant grows rooted in the mud of ponds and lakes.
quiz.mistake: Does not link floating leaves with a water habitat

teach.ask: Gappu fans himself: 'I'd melt in a desert! How does a camel live there, and what's this word adaptation?'
teach.praise: Wow! The camel has long legs, padded feet and a fat-storing hump. Every animal has adaptations to survive in its home!
teach.nudge: But what special features does the camel have? And why do they help it survive?

chapters.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

learn.hook: Your plate of dal, rice and sabzi is actually a team of tiny helpers. Each one has a job to do in your body!
points: Nutrients are the parts of food our body needs to stay healthy.
Carbohydrates (rice, wheat roti, potato, millets like ragi and bajra) give us energy. Fats (ghee, butter, oil, nuts) give even more energy.
Proteins (dal, rajma, milk, paneer, eggs, fish, soybean) are body-building foods: they help us grow and repair the body.
Vitamins and minerals (fruits, vegetables, milk) protect us from diseases and keep the body working well.
Dietary fibre (roughage) in whole grains, fruits and vegetables helps the body get rid of undigested food. Water helps carry nutrients and remove wastes as sweat and urine.

example.q: Aman plays football for two hours every evening. Which nutrient does he mainly need for energy, and from which food?
steps: Running and kicking use a lot of energy.
Carbohydrates and fats are energy-giving nutrients.
Foods like rice, roti, potato and millets are rich in carbohydrates.
example.answer: Carbohydrates, from foods like rice, roti and millets (fats also give energy).

learn.reallife: In school, with a teacher, a drop of dilute iodine solution on a potato slice turns it blue-black, showing starch (a carbohydrate). Rubbing a groundnut on paper leaves an oily patch that light shines through, showing fat. Never taste or play with lab chemicals.

games.title: Which nutrient is it rich in?
Match the nutrient to its job
pairs: help us grow and repair the body

quiz.q: Which nutrient helps our body grow and repair itself?
quiz.explain: Proteins are called body-building foods because they help in growth and repair.
quiz.mistake: Thinks energy foods are the body-building foods

quiz.q: Which food is rich in carbohydrates?
quiz.explain: Rice contains a lot of starch, which is a carbohydrate.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up carbohydrate foods with protein or fat foods

quiz.q: Which food is a good source of protein?
quiz.explain: Pulses like moong dal are rich in protein.
quiz.mistake: Does not know pulses are protein-rich

quiz.q: Which nutrient gives the MOST energy for the same amount of food?
quiz.explain: Fats give more than twice the energy of the same weight of carbohydrates or proteins.
quiz.mistake: Thinks vitamins or proteins are the biggest energy source

quiz.q: What does dietary fibre (roughage) do?
options: Helps the body get rid of undigested food
quiz.explain: Fibre adds bulk and helps undigested food move out of the body, preventing constipation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fibre is an energy or body-building nutrient

quiz.q: Which test result shows that a food contains starch?
options: It leaves an oily patch on paper
It turns blue-black with dilute iodine solution
quiz.explain: Starch turns blue-black when a drop of dilute iodine solution is added.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the starch test with the fat test

quiz.q: Rubbing a groundnut on paper leaves a patch that light shines through. What does this show?
quiz.explain: An oily patch that lets light through shows that fat is present.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the paper test shows starch

quiz.q: Why do we need water even though it gives no energy?
options: It helps carry nutrients and remove wastes
It gives more energy than fat
quiz.explain: Water helps the body absorb nutrients and remove wastes through sweat and urine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only energy-giving foods are useful

teach.ask: Gappu stares at his plate: 'Why can't I eat only sweets all day? What do different foods do for my body?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Carbs and fats give energy, proteins build the body, vitamins and minerals protect me. Sweets alone can't do all that!
teach.nudge: Which food helps me grow, and which food keeps me from getting sick?

learn.hook: A cricket team needs batters, bowlers and a keeper. Your meal also needs a full team of nutrients!
points: A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, along with fibre and water.
How much food we need depends on our age, how active we are and our health. A growing child and a farmer need plenty of energy.
Indian meals like dal-chawal with sabzi and curd, or roti with dal and salad, can be nicely balanced.
Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are nutritious grains. The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets.
Mindful eating means eating slowly, chewing well, stopping when full, eating fresh home-cooked food, eating less junk food and not wasting food.

example.q: Priya's lunch is only puri and aloo sabzi, with a glass of cola. How can she make it balanced?
steps: Puri (fried) and potato give carbohydrates and fat, which are energy.
Missing: protein, enough vitamins and minerals, and fibre. Cola adds lots of sugar.
Add dal or curd for protein, a salad or green vegetable for vitamins and fibre, and drink water instead of cola.
example.answer: Add dal or curd, a green vegetable or salad, and choose water instead of cola.

learn.reallife: Each region of India has its own balanced meals: idli-sambar in the south, dal-baati in Rajasthan, fish-rice in Bengal and makki roti with sarson saag in Punjab.

games.title: Healthy plate: true or false?
items: A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right amounts.
Eating only chips and soft drinks every day is a balanced diet.
These foods have too much fat, salt or sugar and lack many nutrients.
Ragi, jowar and bajra are millets.
These are nutritious millet grains grown in India.
Chewing food well and eating slowly is part of mindful eating.
It helps digestion and tells us when we are full.
All people need exactly the same amount of food.
Needs depend on age, activity and health.
The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets.
2023 was celebrated as the International Year of Millets.

options: Food with all nutrients in the right amounts, plus fibre and water

quiz.mistake: Thinks one kind of nutrient is enough

options: Roti, dal, green sabzi, salad and curd
quiz.explain: This meal has carbohydrates (roti), protein (dal, curd), vitamins, minerals and fibre (sabzi, salad).
quiz.mistake: Picks a meal that tastes good but lacks nutrients

quiz.explain: Ragi (finger millet) is a millet. Rice and wheat are other cereals, and potato is a tuber.

quiz.q: Why should we eat junk food only rarely?
options: It is very rich in fibre
It has too much fat, salt or sugar and few useful nutrients
quiz.explain: Junk food fills us up with fat, salt and sugar but lacks proteins, vitamins and fibre.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tasty food is always nutritious

quiz.q: Which is an example of mindful eating?
options: Eating very fast while watching a screen
Eating slowly and stopping when you feel full
quiz.explain: Paying attention while eating helps digestion and stops overeating.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what mindful eating means

quiz.q: Who needs more energy-giving food?
options: A farmer ploughing a field all day
A person sitting still for an hour
quiz.explain: Hard physical work uses more energy, so a farmer working all day needs more energy food.
quiz.mistake: Thinks everyone needs the same amount of food

quiz.q: The International Year of Millets was in which year?
quiz.explain: The United Nations named 2023 the International Year of Millets.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the year

quiz.q: Which habit helps reduce food waste?
options: Taking a big helping and leaving most of it
Cooking food and throwing it away
Taking only as much food as you can eat
quiz.explain: Taking small helpings and asking for more if needed means less food is thrown away.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect serving size with waste

teach.ask: Gappu's tummy rumbles: 'I eat only grains all day. My friend says I need a balanced diet. What does that mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, plus fibre and water. I'll add some greens to my grains!
teach.nudge: Do I need just one kind of nutrient, or many? And how much of each?

learn.hook: If your body misses one tiny vitamin for a long time, it can show signs like weak bones or bleeding gums. Good food fixes it!
points: A deficiency disease happens when the body does not get enough of a nutrient for a long time.
Vitamin A: poor eyesight, especially night blindness (eat carrots, papaya, mango, milk). Vitamin B1: beriberi, weak muscles (eat whole grains, pulses).
Vitamin C: scurvy, bleeding gums (eat amla, guava, oranges, lemons). Vitamin D: rickets, soft and bent bones (sunlight, milk, eggs, fish).
Calcium: weak bones and teeth (milk, curd, ragi). Iodine: goitre, a swelling in the neck (iodised salt). Iron: anaemia, feeling tired and weak (green leafy vegetables, pulses).
Deficiency diseases can be prevented by eating a balanced diet.

example.q: Raju's gums bleed often. His doctor says he needs more of a certain vitamin. Which vitamin, and what should he eat?
steps: Bleeding gums are a sign of scurvy.
Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits, amla and guava.
example.answer: Vitamin C; he should eat amla, guava, oranges or lemons.

learn.reallife: Common table salt in India is often iodised to prevent goitre, and many children get vitamin D by playing in the morning sunshine.

games.title: Match the deficiency to the disease

items.q: Bleeding gums: which vitamin is lacking?
Night blindness: which vitamin is lacking?
Feeling tired due to anaemia: which mineral is lacking?
Mineral for strong bones and teeth?

quiz.q: What causes a deficiency disease?
options: Lack of a nutrient in the diet for a long time
quiz.explain: Deficiency diseases are caused by not getting enough of a nutrient over a long time, not by germs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all diseases spread from person to person

quiz.q: Lack of vitamin C causes:
quiz.explain: Scurvy, with bleeding gums, is caused by a lack of vitamin C.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the vitamins and their diseases

quiz.q: A child with soft, bent bones may have rickets. Which vitamin is lacking?
quiz.explain: Vitamin D helps the body use calcium for strong bones. Its lack causes rickets.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up vitamin D with other vitamins

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by a lack of iodine?

quiz.mistake: Confuses mineral and vitamin deficiencies

quiz.q: Which food is a rich source of vitamin C?
quiz.explain: Amla (Indian gooseberry) is very rich in vitamin C.
quiz.mistake: Picks an energy food instead of a protective food

quiz.q: Night blindness is caused by a lack of:
quiz.explain: Vitamin A keeps our eyes healthy. Its lack causes night blindness.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the vitamin needed for eyes

quiz.q: Meena feels tired and weak all the time, and her doctor says she has anaemia. What should she eat more of?
options: Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables
quiz.explain: Anaemia is often caused by a lack of iron. Green leafy vegetables and pulses provide iron.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sugary food will cure tiredness

quiz.q: How can deficiency diseases be prevented?
quiz.explain: A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients, so no deficiency develops.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect a balanced diet with preventing disease

teach.ask: Gappu looks worried: 'My cousin's gums bleed. Is it a germ? How can food make someone sick or well?'
teach.praise: Phew! It's a deficiency, not a germ. Eating a balanced diet with all vitamins and minerals keeps such diseases away!
teach.nudge: But what is missing in the body? And how can we stop it from happening?

learn.hook: Why does a fridge magnet stick to the fridge door but not to a wooden table? Let's find out!
points: A magnet attracts (pulls) some materials towards itself.
Materials attracted by a magnet are magnetic materials: iron, nickel and cobalt (and things made mostly of iron).
Materials not attracted by a magnet are non-magnetic: wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, cloth, and metals like copper, aluminium, gold and silver.
Not every metal is magnetic! A copper wire or aluminium foil is not pulled by a magnet.
Long ago, people found a natural magnet called magnetite (lodestone), a rock that attracts iron. Today most magnets are made by people, in shapes like bar, U-shaped (horseshoe), ring and disc.

example.q: Kavya mixes iron pins and plastic beads by mistake. How can she separate them quickly?
steps: Iron is a magnetic material; plastic is not.
Move a magnet over the mixture.
The iron pins stick to the magnet and the plastic beads stay behind.
example.answer: Use a magnet to pick up the iron pins.

learn.reallife: Scrap dealers (kabadiwalas) and recycling plants use big magnets to separate iron scrap from other waste.

quiz.q: Which of these is attracted by a magnet?
quiz.explain: Iron is a magnetic material, so the nail is pulled by the magnet.
quiz.mistake: Does not know which materials are magnetic

quiz.explain: Copper is a metal, but it is non-magnetic.

quiz.explain: Magnetite, also called lodestone, is a naturally found rock that attracts iron.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all magnets are made by people

quiz.explain: Wood, plastic, glass and copper are examples of non-magnetic materials.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two terms

quiz.explain: Iron, nickel and cobalt are all attracted by a magnet.
quiz.mistake: Includes non-magnetic metals in the magnetic group

options: Move a magnet through the sand
quiz.explain: The magnet attracts the iron pins, leaving the sand behind.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the magnetic property for separation

quiz.explain: A U-shaped magnet is called a horseshoe magnet.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the names of magnet shapes

quiz.q: Will a magnet pick up an aluminium soft-drink can?
options: Only if the can is empty
quiz.explain: Aluminium is a metal but it is not attracted by a magnet.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shiny metal objects are always magnetic

teach.ask: Gappu holds a magnet near a spoon, a coin and a crayon: 'Why do some things jump to my magnet and others don't?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Magnets attract magnetic materials like iron, nickel and cobalt. Wood, plastic and even copper are non-magnetic!
teach.nudge: Which materials does a magnet attract? Are all metals attracted?

learn.hook: Two magnets can hug each other or push each other away. It all depends on which ends meet!
points: Every magnet has two poles: a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).
The attraction of a magnet is strongest near its poles. Iron filings collect most at the ends of a bar magnet.
Like poles repel (N–N or S–S push apart). Unlike poles attract (N–S pull together).
A freely hanging bar magnet always comes to rest pointing in the north–south direction.
If you break a magnet, each piece still has both a north and a south pole. You can never get a magnet with just one pole!

example.q: Rahul brings the N pole of one bar magnet near the N pole of another. What will he feel? What if he turns one magnet around?
steps: N and N are like poles.
Like poles repel, so he will feel the magnets pushing apart.
If he turns one magnet, N faces S. Unlike poles attract, so they pull together.
example.answer: First they repel; after turning one magnet around, they attract.

learn.reallife: Magnetic toys and the doors of some cupboards use attraction between unlike poles to snap shut.

quiz.q: How many poles does every magnet have?
quiz.explain: Every magnet has two poles: north and south.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a magnet can have one pole

quiz.q: What happens when the south pole of one magnet comes near the south pole of another?
quiz.explain: Like poles repel each other.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all poles attract each other

quiz.q: Where is the attraction of a bar magnet the strongest?
quiz.explain: Iron filings gather mostly at the ends, showing the poles are strongest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the middle of the magnet is the strongest

quiz.q: A bar magnet is hung freely by a thread. In which direction will it come to rest?
quiz.explain: A freely suspended magnet always settles pointing north–south.
quiz.mistake: Does not know a free magnet aligns north–south

quiz.q: Anu breaks a bar magnet into two pieces. What does each piece have?

quiz.explain: Each piece becomes a complete magnet with two poles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks breaking separates the north and south poles

quiz.q: Which pair of poles will attract each other?
options: None of the poles ever attract
quiz.explain: Unlike poles (N and S) attract each other.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up like and unlike poles

quiz.q: Which is the surest test that an object is a magnet?
options: It is attracted by a magnet
It repels one pole of a known magnet
quiz.explain: Iron is attracted by a magnet too, but only a magnet can repel another magnet. Repulsion is the sure test.
quiz.mistake: Thinks attraction alone proves something is a magnet

quiz.q: Ravi has a magnet with its labels rubbed off. How can he find its north pole?
options: Hang it freely; the end that points north is its north pole
quiz.explain: A freely hanging magnet points north–south. The end pointing north is the north pole.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the north–south property

teach.ask: Gappu pushes two magnets together: 'Sometimes they stick, sometimes they run away from each other! Why?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Same poles push apart, opposite poles pull together. My magnets aren't moody after all!
teach.nudge: What happens with two same poles, and what happens with two different poles?

topics.title: The compass and caring for magnets

learn.hook: Lost in a forest with no phone? A tiny magnetic needle can show you the way!
points: A magnetic compass has a small magnetic needle that can turn freely. It comes to rest pointing north–south.
The north-pointing end of the needle is usually painted or marked so we can read the direction.
Sailors and travellers used compasses to find directions. Sailors and pilots still carry them.
We can make a magnet: stroke an iron nail many times from one end to the other with one pole of a magnet, always in the same direction.
Magnets lose their magnetism if heated, hammered or dropped. Store bar magnets in pairs with unlike poles side by side, with pieces of soft iron (keepers) across the ends.

example.q: The marked north end of Ishaan's compass needle points towards the big banyan tree near his house. In which direction is the tree from him?
steps: A compass needle settles in the north–south direction.
Check the marked (north) end of the needle.
The marked end points to the banyan tree, so the tree lies to the north of him.
example.answer: The tree is to the north of Ishaan.

learn.reallife: Ships crossing the Arabian Sea and trekkers in the Himalayas carry compasses, because a compass needs no battery or signal.

quiz.explain: Like a freely hanging bar magnet, the magnetic needle comes to rest in the north–south direction.

quiz.explain: Far out at sea there are no landmarks, so a compass shows the directions.
quiz.mistake: Does not see where finding direction matters

options: Back and forth in both directions
With the same pole, in one direction, many times
By hitting it with the magnet
quiz.explain: Stroking in only one direction, many times, lines up the nail's magnetism.

options: Heating it or dropping it often
Keeping it in a dry box
quiz.explain: Heat, hammering and dropping make a magnet lose its magnetism.
quiz.mistake: Confuses good storage with things that harm magnets

quiz.q: How should two bar magnets be stored?
options: Thrown loosely in a drawer with keys
Side by side with unlike poles together, with keepers across the ends
quiz.explain: Unlike poles side by side with soft-iron keepers help magnets keep their strength.

options: It will turn towards or away from the magnet
quiz.explain: The needle is a magnet, so it is attracted or repelled by the nearby magnet and stops showing the correct north.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the needle itself is a magnet

quiz.q: The marked end of a compass needle points towards a temple. In which direction is the temple?
quiz.explain: The marked end of the needle points north, so the temple is to the north.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the marked end points south

quiz.q: Why do compasses still matter even though we have phones with maps?
options: A compass works without battery or signal
quiz.explain: In forests, mountains or at sea there may be no signal or charge, but a compass still works.
quiz.mistake: Thinks old tools are useless now

teach.ask: Gappu is lost on a picnic: 'Everyone says use a compass! How can that little needle tell me where north is?'
teach.praise: Hooray! The compass needle is a tiny magnet that turns freely and settles north–south. I can find my way home!
teach.nudge: What is the needle made of, and in which direction does it settle?

learn.hook: If you measure a table with your handspan and your little brother measures it with his, you'll get different answers. Who is right?
points: Long ago people measured length with body parts: handspan, cubit (elbow to fingertip), foot, pace (step) and angul (finger width). In ancient India, units like angul and dhanush were used.
Body measures differ from person to person, so the same object gives different results.
So the world agreed on standard units. The SI unit (International System of Units) of length is the metre (m).
1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm); 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres (mm); 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres.
We choose the unit to suit the length: mm for a pencil tip, cm for a book, m for a room, km for the distance between cities.

example.q: Tanvi's ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?
steps: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 200 cm.
Add the extra 35 cm: 200 + 35.
example.answer: 235 cm

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers measure cloth in metres, road signs show distances in kilometres, and your school ruler shows centimetres and millimetres.

quiz.q: What is the SI unit of length?
quiz.explain: The metre is the standard (SI) unit of length. Centimetre and kilometre are made from it.
quiz.mistake: Picks a smaller or bigger unit instead of the base SI unit

quiz.q: Why are handspans not good for measuring accurately?
options: Different people have different handspan lengths
Handspans are not allowed in India
quiz.explain: Each person's handspan is a different length, so results do not match.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the problem of non-standard units

quiz.q: How many centimetres are there in 4 m?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 10 or 1000 instead of 100

quiz.q: How many millimetres are in 7 cm?
quiz.explain: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 7 cm = 7 × 10 = 70 mm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 100 instead of 10 for cm to mm
steps: 1 cm = 10 mm

quiz.q: Ravi's school is 3 km from home. How far is that in metres?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by 100 instead of 1000

quiz.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a pencil?
quiz.explain: A pencil is about 15 to 20 cm long, so centimetres suit it best.
quiz.mistake: Does not match the unit size to the object

quiz.q: Which old unit is the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger?
quiz.explain: A cubit is measured from the elbow to the fingertip.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of body measures

quiz.q: A rope is 1 m 50 cm long. How many centimetres is that?
quiz.mistake: Writes the numbers side by side instead of converting

teach.ask: Gappu measures a twig with his tiny claw: 'It's 12 claws long! But my friend the crow says it's 5 claws. Who's right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Claws and handspans are different for everyone. Using a standard unit like the metre means everyone gets the same answer!
teach.nudge: Why do our claw measurements differ? What unit should we both use?

learn.hook: A ruler is only as good as the person using it. A tiny slip of the eye can change your answer!
points: Place the scale along the length of the object, touching it.
Start from the zero mark. If the zero mark is broken, start from another full mark (like 1 cm) and subtract it from the final reading.
Keep your eye directly above the point you are reading. Looking from the side gives a wrong reading.
To measure a curved line, lay a thread along it, mark the ends, straighten the thread and measure it with a scale.
Choose the right tool: a ruler for a book, a measuring tape for your waist or a tree trunk, a metre scale for a door.

example.q: Sameer's ruler has a broken edge, so he places a pencil starting at the 2.0 cm mark. The other end is at 11.5 cm. How long is the pencil?
steps: The pencil starts at 2.0 cm, not at 0.
Length = end reading − start reading.
example.answer: 9.5 cm

learn.reallife: Tailors use a soft measuring tape around your shoulders and waist, and carpenters use a metal tape to measure wood before cutting.

teach.praise: Got it! Keep the scale along the crayon, start at zero (or subtract the start) and look straight down. Now my reading won't wobble!
teach.nudge: Where should I keep my eyes? And where should I start measuring from?

learn.hook: A cricket ball flies, a fan spins, a swing goes back and forth. Everything is moving, but in different ways!
points: An object is in motion if its position changes with time compared to its surroundings; otherwise it is at rest.
Linear motion: moving along a straight line, like a train on a straight track, a falling stone, or a sprinter in a 100 m race.
Circular motion: moving along a circle around a centre, like the tip of a fan blade, a giant wheel at a mela, or a stone tied to a string and whirled.
Periodic motion: a motion that repeats itself after fixed intervals of time, like a swinging pendulum, a jhula going to and fro, or the hands of a clock.
Some motions are of more than one type. A fan blade moves in a circle and repeats again and again, so it is both circular and periodic.

example.q: What type of motion does a child on a swing (jhula) have?
steps: The swing goes forward and comes back to the same point.
It repeats this to-and-fro movement again and again, taking about the same time for each swing.
A motion that repeats after fixed time intervals is periodic.
example.answer: Periodic (to-and-fro, or oscillatory) motion

learn.reallife: At a Dussehra or Diwali mela you can spot all three: a toy train on a straight track (linear), a giant wheel (circular) and a pendulum-like boat ride swinging to and fro (periodic).

Motion only in a straight line

learn.hook: Your tiffin box, your chair and your bangles are all objects. But what are they made of? That's the material!
points: An object is a thing (like a spoon or a chair). A material is what it is made of (like steel, wood, plastic or glass).
One object can be made from different materials: a chair can be wooden, plastic or metal. One material can make many objects: wood makes chairs, doors and pencils.
Appearance: materials that shine, like gold, silver, copper and aluminium foil, are called lustrous. Wood, paper, cloth and chalk are non-lustrous.
Metals can lose their shine in air and moisture; a copper vessel turns dull but shines again after cleaning.
Hardness: hard materials like iron and stone are difficult to scratch or press. Soft materials like cotton and sponge can be pressed easily.

example.q: Nisha has a piece of cotton and a piece of stone. She tries to press both with her fingers. Which is hard and which is soft?

learn.hook: Sugar disappears in water, oil floats on top, and you can see through glass but not through a wall. Materials behave differently!
points: Soluble materials dissolve (mix completely) in water, like sugar and salt. Insoluble ones do not, like sand, chalk powder and sawdust.
Some liquids mix with water (lemon juice, vinegar); some do not (oil forms a layer on top).
Some objects float on water (a dry leaf, a piece of wood, a cork); others sink (a stone, an iron nail, a glass marble).
Transparent materials let us see clearly through them (clear glass, clean water, air).
Translucent materials let us see only partly (butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper). Opaque materials do not let us see through at all (wood, cardboard, a metal sheet).

example.q: Raj adds a spoon of sand and a spoon of salt to two glasses of water and stirs. What will he see?

learn.hook: Can your hands lie to you? Try this and see: the same water can feel warm to one hand and cool to the other!
points: We often say things are hot, warm, cool or cold. Temperature tells us exactly how hot or cold something is.
Our sense of touch is not reliable for judging temperature.

Try this (with an adult): keep one hand in cool tap water and the other in comfortably warm (not hot) water for a minute. Then put both in normal tap water. The 'cool' hand feels it as warm, and the 'warm' hand feels it as cool!
Never test very hot water, a hot iron or a stove with your hand; it can burn you.
To know temperature correctly and safely, we use a thermometer.

example.q: Two friends dip their hands into the same bucket of water. Simran says 'warm!' and Aditya says 'cool!'. How is this possible?
steps: Just before, Simran had her hand in cold water and Aditya had his hand in warm water.
Our skin compares the new water with what it felt just before.
So the same water feels different to each of them.
example.answer: Touch depends on what the hand felt before, so it is not reliable. A thermometer gives the true temperature.

learn.hook: A thermometer is like a truthful friend: it never says 'it feels warm', it tells you the exact number!
points: A clinical thermometer measures body temperature. Its range is usually 35 °C to 42 °C.

A laboratory thermometer measures the temperature of other things like water. Its range is usually −10 °C to 110 °C.
Digital thermometers show the reading as numbers on a screen. Older thermometers had mercury, which is poisonous, so digital ones are now preferred.

Good habits: wash the thermometer before and after use; hold it away from the tip; for a lab thermometer, keep the bulb in the liquid without touching the container and read it while it is still in the liquid.

example.q: Why should a clinical thermometer NOT be used to measure the temperature of boiling water?

example.answer: Its range (35 °C to 42 °C) is too small. Use a laboratory thermometer (with an adult) instead.

chapters.title: A Journey through States of Water

learn.hook: Water is a shape-shifter! It can be a hard ice cube, a splashing liquid or an invisible gas in the air.
points: Water can exist in three states: solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (water vapour).
A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. An ice cube keeps its shape in any glass.
A liquid has a fixed volume but no fixed shape; it takes the shape of its container.
A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume; it spreads out to fill all the space it gets. Water vapour is invisible.
All matter is made of tiny particles. In solids they are packed very close, in liquids a little apart, and in gases far apart and moving freely.

example.q: Rohit pours 200 mL of water from a tall glass into a flat bowl. What changes and what stays the same?
steps: Water is a liquid.
Liquids take the shape of their container, so the shape changes from tall to flat.
Liquids have a fixed volume, so the amount stays 200 mL.
example.answer: The shape changes, but the volume stays 200 mL.

learn.hook: Where does the water from wet clothes go? And where do the drops on a cold glass come from? Same water, opposite journeys!
points: Evaporation: liquid water slowly changes into water vapour from its surface. It happens at all temperatures, not only when water boils.
Evaporation is faster when it is hotter, when there is wind, when the water is spread over a larger area, and when the air is less humid (less moist).
Evaporation causes cooling: sweat cools our body, and water in an earthen matka or surahi stays cool as water seeping through it evaporates.
Condensation: water vapour cools and changes back into liquid water, like droplets on the outside of a cold glass, dew on grass, and a foggy bathroom mirror.
Water cycle: water evaporates from seas, rivers and land, condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds, and falls back as rain, snow or hail.

example.q: Pooja hangs one wet dupatta spread out and another folded, both in the sun. Which dries first, and why?
steps: Both are in the sun, so the temperature is the same.
The spread-out dupatta has a larger surface exposed to air.
A larger surface area makes evaporation faster.

quiz.q: How are clouds formed?
options: Smoke from chimneys collects in the sky
Ice is thrown up from the sea
Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets
quiz.explain: Rising water vapour cools high up and condenses into tiny droplets that make clouds.
quiz.mistake: Does not link clouds with condensation

quiz.q: Why do we feel cool when sweat dries on our skin?

teach.ask: Gappu stares at his empty water dish: 'I left water here this morning. Now it's gone! And why is my cold glass wet outside?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The water in my dish evaporated into vapour, and vapour in the air condensed on the cold glass. Opposite journeys!
teach.nudge: Where did the water in the dish go? And what turns the vapour back into drops?

learn.hook: Leave a kulfi out in May and see how fast it turns into a puddle! That's melting in action.
points: Melting: a solid changes into a liquid on heating. Ice melts at 0 °C.
Freezing: a liquid changes into a solid on cooling. Pure water freezes at 0 °C.
So melting and freezing are opposite changes, and for water both happen at 0 °C.
Boiling: water changes quickly into vapour at 100 °C, with bubbles forming throughout the liquid.
Water expands when it freezes, so ice is lighter than the same volume of water and floats. A glass bottle filled to the top with water can crack in a freezer.

example.q: Ice cubes are put into a glass of water. Do they sink or float, and why?
steps: When water freezes, it expands and takes up more space.
So a piece of ice is lighter than the same volume of water.
Things lighter than the same volume of water float.
example.answer: They float, because ice is lighter than the same volume of water.

learn.reallife: Snow on the Himalayas melts in summer and feeds rivers like the Ganga. Kulfi and ice cream are made by freezing.

pairs: Water to vapour at the surface

Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal air pressure.

teach.nudge: What do we call ice turning into water? And what about water turning into ice? At what temperature?

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

learn.hook: Nani picks tiny stones out of the dal before cooking. She's doing science: separating a mixture!
points: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together. We separate them to remove unwanted or harmful parts, or to get useful parts.
Handpicking: picking out by hand things that are big enough to see and few in number, like stones from rice or dal.
Threshing: separating grains from their stalks by beating them, using animals, or using threshing machines.
Winnowing: dropping a mixture from a height in the wind. Light husk blows away; heavy grains fall close by. A soop (winnowing basket) is often used.
Sieving: passing a mixture through a sieve (chhalni). Fine particles pass through; bigger ones stay behind, like bran from flour or pebbles from sand.

example.q: Grandpa has a sack of wheat grains mixed with light, dry husk. Which method should he use, and how does it work?
steps: The husk is much lighter than the grains.
Winnowing uses wind to separate light and heavy parts.
He drops the mixture slowly from a height on a windy day: husk blows away, grains fall in a heap below.
example.answer: Winnowing

learn.reallife: At a construction site, workers pass sand through a big slanting wire sieve to remove pebbles. At home, flour is sieved before making rotis.

games.title: Which method?
pairs: Pulling iron pins out of sand

learn.hook: Muddy water from a village pond can be made clearer, step by step. Let's see how!
points: Sedimentation: when muddy water is left undisturbed, the heavier insoluble particles slowly settle at the bottom. The settled layer is called sediment.
Decantation: gently pouring off the clearer water from the top without disturbing the sediment.
Filtration: passing a mixture through a filter that lets the liquid pass but stops the solid particles. Examples: tea strainer, filter paper, a clean cotton cloth.
The clear liquid that passes through is called the filtrate; the solid left behind is the residue.
Filtered water may still have germs that we cannot see. It must be boiled or purified before drinking.

example.q: While making paneer, Ammi adds lemon juice to hot milk (adult job!). Soft lumps form in a watery liquid. How can the paneer be separated?
steps: The lumps (chhena) are solid; the watery part (whey) is liquid.
Pour the mixture through a clean muslin cloth.
The whey passes through; the paneer stays in the cloth.
example.answer: Filtration through a muslin cloth

learn.reallife: Tea is filtered through a strainer every morning. Water purifiers at home and big water treatment plants use settling and filtering before cleaning the water further.

quiz.explain: Removing most of the mud first means the filter only has to catch the smaller particles left behind.

teach.ask: Gappu looks at a muddy puddle: 'I'm thirsty! How can I get the mud out of this water? Is clear water safe to drink?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Let the mud settle, pour off the water, filter it, and boil it before drinking. Clean water at last!
teach.nudge: After the mud settles, what do I do next? And is filtered water fully safe?

topics.title: Evaporation, churning and using methods together

learn.hook: How do we get salt from the salty sea? The Sun helps us do it!
points: Evaporation can separate a solid dissolved in water: when the water evaporates, the solid is left behind.
Salt is made this way in salt pans along the coasts of states like Gujarat: seawater is let into shallow pans and the Sun evaporates the water, leaving salt.
Churning: curd or cream is churned (stirred hard) with a mathani or a churner. Butter, which is lighter, collects on top and is separated from buttermilk (chhaas).
Sometimes we use more than one method. Salt and sand: add water to dissolve the salt, filter out the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt back.
Safety: heating to evaporate should only be done by or with an adult.

example.q: Sana accidentally mixes salt with sand. How can she get both back?
steps: Add water and stir: salt dissolves, sand does not.
Filter the mixture: sand stays on the filter paper as residue.
Leave the salty filtrate in a shallow dish in the sun (or let an adult heat it) so the water evaporates.
Salt is left behind in the dish.
example.answer: Dissolve in water, filter to get the sand, then evaporate the water to get the salt.

learn.reallife: Making butter by churning curd is common in many Indian homes, and the leftover chhaas is a cool summer drink.

learn.hook: A toy car moves, a cloud grows bigger, a candle 'breathes' air to burn. Are they alive? Let's find the real test!
points: Living things need food, water and air to live.
Living things breathe (take in air) and get energy from food. This is called respiration.
Living things grow, respond to changes around them (stimuli), get rid of wastes (excretion) and reproduce (make young ones of their own kind).
Most animals move from place to place; plants show movement too, like a chhui-mui (touch-me-not) folding its leaves when touched.
Living things have a life span: they are born, grow, grow old and die. Non-living things may show one or two of these features, but never all of them.

example.q: A car moves and uses fuel. Is it a living thing?
steps: A car moves and uses fuel, so it shows some features.
But it does not grow, breathe, reproduce or respond to touch on its own.
A living thing must show all the features of life.
example.answer: No. A car is non-living; it shows only a few features, not all.

learn.reallife: When you water a wilting tulsi plant and it perks up, or a puppy runs to you when called, you are seeing living things respond.

quiz.mistake: Picks a feature found in only some living things

quiz.explain: Folding leaves after a touch is a response to a stimulus.
quiz.mistake: Thinks plants cannot respond

options: It does not breathe, eat or reproduce
quiz.explain: Growing alone is not enough. A cloud does not show the other features of life.

quiz.explain: Excretion removes harmful waste materials from the body.

quiz.explain: A bicycle can be moved, but it does not breathe, grow or reproduce.

quiz.mistake: Thinks only animals breathe

teach.ask: Gappu points at a moving car and a sleeping cat: 'The car moves and the cat is still. So is the car alive and the cat not?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Moving is not enough. The cat eats, breathes, grows, responds and has kittens. The car does none of that!
teach.nudge: What features must a living thing show? Does the car grow or have babies?

topics.title: Seeds and plants are alive too

learn.hook: A tiny dry moong seed looks lifeless. Add water, and in two days it sprouts! Was it alive all along?
points: A seed is a living thing that is resting. When conditions are right, it wakes up and starts to grow. This is called germination.
Seeds need water, air and a suitable (warm, not too cold) temperature to germinate.
Seeds kept dry do not germinate. Seeds kept fully under water (without air) usually do not germinate either. Seeds kept in a fridge germinate poorly or not at all.
Most seeds like moong and chana can germinate even in the dark.
Plants grow, take in air through tiny pores in their leaves, make their own food in sunlight, respond (roots grow towards water, shoots towards light) and make seeds.

example.q: Arnav sets up three cups of moong seeds: A dry, B on wet cotton, C fully under water. Which sprout well and why?
steps: Cup A has air and warmth but no water: no sprouting.
Cup B has water, air and warmth: good sprouting.
Cup C has water but very little air: little or no sprouting.
example.answer: Only cup B sprouts well, because seeds need water, air and suitable warmth.

learn.reallife: Moong and chana sprouts are a healthy breakfast in many Indian homes. Soaking and keeping them in a damp cloth gives them water, air and warmth to germinate.

learn.hook: A frog was once a tiny tadpole with a tail, and a butterfly was once a crawling caterpillar. Life is full of surprises!
points: A life cycle is the series of stages a living thing goes through from birth to becoming an adult that can produce young ones.
Frog: egg → tadpole (lives in water, has a tail, breathes with gills) → froglet (grows legs) → adult frog.
Mosquito: egg → larva → pupa → adult. The eggs, larvae and pupae live in still (stagnant) water, so we must not let water collect in coolers, pots or tyres.
Butterfly: egg → caterpillar (larva) → pupa (also called a chrysalis) → adult butterfly. Big changes in body shape like these are called metamorphosis.
Plant: seed → seedling → young plant → adult plant with flowers → fruits with seeds → new plants.

example.q: Why do health workers ask people to empty water from coolers and old tyres every week, especially in the rainy season?
steps: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water.
The larvae and pupae also grow in that water before becoming adults.
Emptying the water breaks the life cycle, so fewer mosquitoes are born.
example.answer: To stop mosquitoes from breeding, by removing the still water their eggs, larvae and pupae need.

learn.reallife: During the monsoon you may see tadpoles in puddles and ponds. Silk is made from the cocoons that silkworms spin when they become pupae; they later turn into moths.

quiz.q: What is the larva of a butterfly called?

quiz.q: Which stage comes just before the adult in a mosquito's life cycle?

quiz.q: What is metamorphosis?

quiz.mistake: Does not know the term

quiz.q: Which is the correct life cycle of a plant?

teach.ask: Gappu sees tadpoles in a pond: 'Mama Frog says these wiggly things are her babies! But they don't look like frogs at all. How?'
teach.praise: Ribbit-tweet! Egg, tadpole, froglet, frog. The babies change shape as they grow: that's a life cycle with metamorphosis!

learn.hook: The air you breathe, the water you drink and the sunshine on your face are gifts from nature. They are nature's treasures!
points: Natural resources are useful things we get from nature, like air, water, sunlight, soil, forests, minerals, coal and petroleum.
Things made by people from natural resources, like plastic, glass, paper and cement, are human-made materials.

Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, with small amounts of others like carbon dioxide and water vapour. We need oxygen to breathe; plants use carbon dioxide to make food.
Soil forms very, very slowly as rocks break down over many years; it holds plants and gives them water and minerals.
The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth: it gives light and warmth, and plants use sunlight to make food.

example.q: Is a wooden chair a natural resource?
steps: The wood comes from trees in forests, which are natural resources.
But the chair itself was cut, shaped and joined by people.
So the wood is natural, while the chair is a human-made object.
example.answer: No. The wood is a natural resource, but the chair is made by people from it.

learn.reallife: Farmers depend on soil, water and sunlight; fishing families on the coast of Kerala depend on the sea; and the paper in your notebook came from trees.

learn.hook: Some treasures refill themselves, like sunlight every day. Others took millions of years to form and will run out!
points: Renewable resources are replaced by nature in a short time, or will not run out: sunlight, wind, and water (renewed by the water cycle). Forests are renewable only if we plant new trees as we cut.
Non-renewable resources took a very long time to form and cannot be replaced quickly once used up: coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are called fossil fuels. They formed from the remains of plants and animals buried deep under the Earth over millions of years.
Burning fossil fuels gives energy but also releases smoke and gases that pollute air.
Solar panels and windmills use renewable energy. India has big solar parks and wind farms.

learn.hook: If we keep taking from nature's treasure box without care, it will become empty. Let's be smart treasure keepers!
points: Conservation means using natural resources carefully so they last for future generations.
Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (make new things from old) help save resources.
Save water: turn off taps, fix leaks, and collect rainwater (rainwater harvesting). Save electricity: switch off lights and fans when not needed.
Plant trees and protect forests. In the 1970s, villagers in the hills of present-day Uttarakhand hugged trees to stop them from being cut; this was the Chipko movement.
Walk, cycle or use public transport for short trips to save fuel and keep the air cleaner.

example.q: Anu's family wants to save water at home. Which ideas work?
steps: Turn off the tap while brushing teeth.

Use a bucket instead of a running hose to wash the car, and reuse water from washing vegetables to water plants.
example.answer: All of these save water: closing taps, fixing leaks and reusing water.

learn.hook: On a clear night away from city lights, you can see thousands of stars. Some of them even make pictures in the sky!
points: Stars are huge balls of very hot gases that give out their own light and heat.
The Sun is a star. It looks big and bright because it is the star nearest to Earth; other stars look like tiny dots because they are very, very far away.

A constellation is a group of stars that seems to form a pattern or shape. Examples: Orion (also called Mriga), Ursa Major (whose seven bright stars are called Saptarishi or the Big Dipper) and Cassiopeia (shaped like a W or M).
The Pole Star (Dhruva tara) stays almost in the same place in the northern sky all night. Two stars of the Saptarishi, called pointer stars, point towards it.
Stars seem to move from east to west across the night sky because the Earth rotates from west to east. Bright city lights (light pollution) make stars hard to see.

example.q: Kunal sees stars during the night but not during the day. Do the stars disappear in the daytime?
steps: Stars are still in the sky during the day.
The Sun is so bright that its light makes the sky bright.
The faint light of distant stars cannot be seen against the bright sky.
example.answer: No. The stars are there, but the bright sunlight hides them.

learn.reallife: Sailors and travellers once used the Pole Star to find the north direction at night. Today, stargazing camps in places like Ladakh, far from city lights, let people see the Milky Way.

learn.hook: Our Earth is part of a giant family that circles around the Sun. Meet the family!
points: The Solar System has the Sun at its centre, with eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets going around it.
The eight planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Planets do not make their own light; they shine by reflecting sunlight. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite and also shines with reflected sunlight.

Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet and the brightest planet in our night sky. Mars looks reddish. Jupiter is the largest planet. Saturn has beautiful rings.
Earth is the only planet known to have life. Since 2006, Pluto has been called a dwarf planet. Many asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

example.q: Lata says, 'The Moon is a star because it shines at night.' Is she right?
steps: Stars make their own light.
The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.

example.answer: No. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, which shines by reflecting sunlight.

learn.hook: India sent a spacecraft to Mars on its very first try and landed near the Moon's south pole. Let's meet India's space heroes!
points: ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) was set up in 1969. Dr Vikram Sarabhai is called the father of the Indian space programme.
Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was launched in 1975. Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to travel to space in 1984.
Chandrayaan-1 (2008) helped discover water molecules on the Moon. Mangalyaan, the Mars Orbiter Mission, was launched in 2013 and reached Mars orbit in 2014; India succeeded on its first attempt.

Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, and the rover Pragyan explored the surface. India was the first country to land near the south pole. 23 August is now National Space Day in India.
Aditya-L1, launched in September 2023, is India's first mission to study the Sun. Many ISRO rockets are launched from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh.

example.answer: Aryabhata (1975) → Mangalyaan (2013) → Chandrayaan-3 landing (2023)
